d1_L_0.quote: Madame plays well. I have heard her many times, and I know the sound of her hands on the keys.
d1_L_0.fact: The sheet says only that the household heard Madame's piano begin and stop by the kitchen clock. It does not say who was playing.
d1_L_0.misreading: A solver could take this to mean Madame was the one playing from 10:48 to 11:01, which gives her a whereabouts and an alibi-relevant identity the sheet never supplies.

d0_L_3.quote: From the kitchen we heard Madame's piano begin at twelve minutes to eleven by the kitchen clock, and stop at one minute past eleven by the kitchen clock.
d0_L_3.fact: The only clock whose error is given is Rosa's clock, which is exactly fifteen minutes fast (L4). The piano readings are given by 'the kitchen clock' (L5). The sheet never says these are the same clock.
d0_L_3.misreading: A careful solver may take 'the kitchen clock' to be a different clock from Rosa's. If so, the fifteen-minute correction would not apply to the piano times, and both piano readings would be attached to the wrong clock. The transcript should have tied the two together, for example by saying the kitchen clock is Rosa's clock.

d1_O_2.quote: He said Jules's watch was a disgrace to the family and that Félix ought to be ashamed to carry it.
d1_O_2.fact: O1 says only that Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine and that Aurèle scolded him for it. It does not mention Jules or say whose watch Félix was carrying.
d1_O_2.misreading: "Ought to be ashamed to carry it" can be read as Félix carrying Jules's watch, which would mean the watch that read twenty minutes to nine belonged to Jules, not Félix. A solver could then attach the 8:40 reading to the wrong man. The sentence should make clear that the disgraceful watch is Félix's own, or that it is a different watch.

d1_O_2.quote: He said Jules's watch was a disgrace to the family and that Félix ought to be ashamed to carry it.
d1_O_2.fact: O1 says only that Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. It does not mention a Jules or say whose watch Félix carried.
d1_O_2.misreading: 'Ought to be ashamed to carry it' can be read as saying Félix was carrying Jules's watch. A careful solver could then conclude the 8:40 reading belonged to Jules's watch, not Félix's, which would attach the reading to the wrong watch.

d0_D_1.quote: She had stopped playing, and we went on with our game.
d0_D_1.fact: D2: Madame began to play the piano as I went out, and she stopped when I came back.
d0_D_1.misreading: The past-perfect 'had stopped' can be read as the piano ending before Vauthier returned to the salon, possibly while he was still in the hall. The fact is that she stopped at the moment he came back, so the order of the piano stopping and his return is unclear.

d0_D_1.quote: It stopped with its master. I say that as a friend and not as a physician.
d0_D_1.fact: The sheet gives no information about the regulator stopping or about when it stopped.
d0_D_1.misreading: A solver could read this as the regulator stopping at the moment of death, and so treat it as a clock reading for the time of death. The sheet supplies no such reading.

d0_D_1.quote: It stopped with its master. I say that as a friend and not as a physician.
d0_D_1.fact: The fact sheet gives no reading or stopping time for the atelier regulator, and says nothing about any clock stopping at the time of death.
d0_D_1.misreading: A solver could take this as a clock that stopped at the moment of death, and so treat the regulator's stopping as a fixed time anchor for the death or for the doctor's whereabouts.

d0_B_0.fact: The fact sheet gives no duration for Girard's time in the library with Félix. It says only that he came back in at 10:46 and went up to Félix in the library, and it gives no departure time.
d0_B_0.misreading: A solver could read 'didn't stay long' as a short visit that ended soon after the 10:50-ish hall-clock reading, and use that to place Girard's departure or Félix's whereabouts at a time the sheet never states.

d0_D_4.quote: A man struck like that would have known very little about it. It would have been very quick.
d0_D_4.fact: The fact sheet gives no information about the assailant's sex or about how long the blow or death took.
d0_D_4.misreading: A solver could take 'A man' as a fact that the killer was male, which could rule out Madame or others. 'Very quick' could be read as a duration hint about the attack or death that the sheet does not support.

d0_D_4.quote: The regulator on the wall had stopped. I thought, God forgive me, that it had stopped with its master.
d0_D_4.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about the atelier regulator, its stopping, or when it stopped.
d0_D_4.misreading: A solver could read 'stopped with its master' as implying the regulator stopped at the moment of death, giving a time of death or a clock reading that is not in the sheet.

d1_F_0.quote: Uncle Aurèle held it up in front of everyone like a dead fish and said it was a wreck and he would not have it in his house.
d1_F_0.fact: The fact sheet gives only F1's reading (twenty to nine at nine o'clock) and says nothing about the accuracy of Félix's watch.
d1_F_0.misreading: The 'wreck' remark, and the later claim that the uncle could 'put it right' and that the repeater was 'the only honest thing in the house, because it told you the time when you asked', imply Félix's silver watch keeps poor time. A solver could discount or adjust every watch reading (9pm, 10pm, 10:15, 10:21, 10:32) and reach different times for the events.

d1_F_2.quote: Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, someone came quickly down. I did not see who that was either.
d1_F_2.fact: F4 places the 10:21 descent after the 10:18 thump, and the 10:15 ascent before it. The fact sheet's sequence is: up at 10:15, thump at 10:18, then down at 10:21.
d1_F_2.misreading: In the transcript the 10:21 descent comes before the piano, the thump, and the repeater. A solver could read the sequence as up at 10:15, down at 10:21, then thump at 10:18, which contradicts the watch readings. Because the thump is at 10:18 and the descent at 10:21, the order of these events decides who could have been on the stairs when the thump happened.

d1_F_2.quote: Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, someone came quickly down. I did not see who that was either. I only heard the feet on the stairs." / "Did you hear anything else before the next thing?" / "...Then, at eighteen minutes past ten by my watch, I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier.
d1_F_2.fact: F4 says the descent at 10:21 came after the 10:15 ascent and that the thump at 10:18 came before the 10:21 descent (the sheet orders the thump between the two stair movements). The fact sheet's 'Before the thump' only applies to the 10:15 ascent.
d1_F_2.misreading: The transcript narrates the 10:21 descent first, then has Matthey ask about 'anything else before the next thing', then gives the thump with 'Then, at eighteen minutes past ten'. A careful solver would read the thump as happening after the descent (10:21), reversing the true order of 10:18 thump and 10:21 descent and changing who could have been on the stairs at the moment of the thump.

d0_F_4.quote: I was one floor below the atelier with a bottle and a dead man's watch in my pocket, and I am the heir.
d0_F_4.fact: F1 and the earlier testimony establish that the watch Félix carries is his father's silver watch, which he has carried since his father died. The uncle is the deceased. The sheet never says Félix has any watch belonging to the victim.
d0_F_4.misreading: The phrase "a dead man's watch" could be read as the uncle's watch, since the uncle is the dead man. A solver might then conclude that the readings Félix gave came from the victim's watch, or that the watch is in question, when the sheet says it was his own watch, his father's.

d1_D_0.quote: It would have been very quick, Inspector.
d1_D_0.fact: The fact sheet gives no duration for anything after the 10:45 departure or any time of death. Its only clock readings are the nine o'clock watch check, the ten o'clock salon clock, and the 10:45 watch reading.
d1_D_0.misreading: A solver could read 'very quick' as a hint that the blow was struck and death followed almost at once, which narrows the time window for the murder to a few moments near a particular clock reading. The sheet supports no such duration.

d1_D_0.quote: But the regulator stopped with its master, and I think that is the truest thing anyone will say tonight.
d1_D_0.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about any clock stopping. Its only clock facts are the watch two minutes fast, the salon clock at 9:55 when the bell struck ten, and the 10:45 watch reading.
d1_D_0.misreading: A solver could take the stopped regulator as a time-of-death marker, or as evidence that a particular clock was halted at the moment of the killing. Either reading would supply a clock reading the sheet does not give.

d1_R_4.quote: The regulator on the wall had stopped.
d1_R_4.fact: The fact sheet gives no information about the wall regulator or when it stopped.
d1_R_4.misreading: A solver could treat the stopped regulator as a time anchor, reading its stoppage as the moment of the death or of the blow, which the sheet does not support and which could conflict with the kitchen-clock readings.

d0_R_0.quote: The regulator on the wall had stopped.
d0_R_0.fact: The fact sheet gives no reading for any stopped clock or time of stopping. R1 to R4 cover only the kitchen clock, the temple, the piano and the hall clock.
d0_R_0.misreading: A solver could take the stopped regulator as a time-of-death or time-of-stopping clue, reading it as an additional clock reading that places the event at a particular moment. The sheet gives no such time.
